subject: history_social
passage: In the 1300s, many towns in Europe began placing mechanical clocks on church towers and town halls. Historian Pieter Claes argues that merchants were the main reason for this change. In his view, merchants wanted a shared way to mark when markets opened and closed, so busy trading towns were the first to pay for public clocks.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Claes's argument?

choices.A: Some of the earliest public clocks struck a bell every hour instead of showing the time on a dial.
choices.B: Records from several trading towns show that merchants paid much of the cost of the first public clocks.
choices.C: Small farming towns with few merchants got public clocks as early as large trading towns did.
choices.D: Public clocks often had to be repaired, because their iron parts wore out quickly.

explanation.why: Claes says merchants drove the spread of public clocks, so trading towns got them first. A finding weakens this if towns without many merchants got clocks just as early, because then merchants could not have been the main reason.
explanation.A: Incorrect. How early clocks signaled the time does not show who wanted them or why.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Merchants paying for the first clocks would support Claes's argument, not weaken it.
explanation.C: Correct. If farming towns with few merchants got clocks as early as trading towns, merchants do not appear to be the main cause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Repairs to clocks say nothing about why towns first installed them.
